text: — I also had a meeting with Bay Ganyo — Kolyo spoke up — in Dresden. — Do you want me to tell it to you?
— "Need you ask? Tell us!" — shouted the whole group.

— I don’t know if you have heard—a few years ago, Dresden society was disturbed by an extremely sad catastrophe, the victims of which were a Bulgarian girl, a student, and a young American. I will remind you of this sad incident in a few words. The Bulgarian girl was studying in Dresden. In this city, as you know, there are entire neighborhoods of English, Americans, Russians, and other foreigners, whose children attend the local educational institutions. An American girl, a student, became friends with our Bulgarian girl. English and American female students have this whim—to take under their patronage some classmate from among the most defenseless. Our Bulgarian girl appeared as such: rather shy, rather meek, rather quiet. They became friends, and the American girl began to invite her to her home as a guest on holidays. The Bulgarian girl met their whole family, and among others, her brother, a young man of twenty, who was studying painting. Who knows whether by the tendency inherent in young artists to be captivated by every living model that does not fit the general type of the models surrounding them, or by the inclination toward originality inherent in Americans, but after several meetings with our modest and shy Bulgarian girl, the young man seemed to begin feeling an attraction toward her; he took every opportunity to meet her, to share his artistic impressions, to be charming—in a word, they began to love each other. And this love shortened their days.

One festive day during the summer holidays, the entire family, accompanied by the Bulgarian woman, set out for a walk through Saxon Switzerland. In a picturesque, rocky area, the young artist, engrossed in conversation with the Bulgarian woman, wandered away from the group. A high cliff caught the young man's eye, and he began to climb it. His companion followed after him: but before they could even reach the middle of the dangerous cliff, the American slipped and, in his fall, dragged the Bulgarian woman into the abyss with him. That was the end of their lives.

The dead pair was brought to Dresden, to the clinic. The whole city was troubled by this mournful event. A multitude of people flocked to see them, laid out side by side on a large marble table. They immediately telegraphed the Bulgarian woman's brother to come to Dresden; she had no closer relatives. The bodies were embalmed to preserve them until his arrival. Numerous wreaths adorned their deathbed. On the third day, a telegram was received from Vienna that the deceased woman's brother was leaving for Dresden. The bodies were moved to the home of the American family. Expecting the brother's arrival with impatience, a multitude of misters and mistresses, a multitude of ladies and gentlemen had gathered in that house. The family belonged to the high society of Dresden. I had gone there too, with a few Bulgarian students. We had invitations as Bulgarians, you know, a deceased Bulgarian woman. Other Bulgarian youths, meanwhile, had gone to the station to meet the deceased's brother. We wait. Mournful solemnity! All the apartments were full of visitors. They spoke quietly, in whispers. The silence was broken from time to time by the bitter sobs and desperate sighs of the grief-stricken mother of the deceased young man. In an interval of dead silence, a terrible clamor was heard from the corridor: a coarse stomping of shoes was heard—as if a shod horse were being led—voices were heard: "Where is it? Is it here?" "Shh!... More quietly!" And into the room of the deceased, with a fur cap on his head, slipped... Bay Ganyo.
— Good day! — he cried out, in a tone and with a facial expression that suggested not so much a mournful mood as indignation; as if the people around him were to blame for his sister's death.

Bay Ganyo approached the deathbed and accidentally pulled back the shroud from the young man's face. — Who is this? What kind of man is this? — he asked, looking over the entire gathering almost fiercely and waiting with fixed eyes for an answer.

A student, a Bulgarian, overcome with shame, approached Bay Ganyo, nudged him lightly by the sleeve, and pulled back the shroud from the face of the deceased woman. Bay Ganyo took off his fur cap, crossed himself, and kissed her on the forehead.

— Oh, the poor soul! What a fate was in store for you... Mariyka, Mariyka! — Bai Ganyo shook his head. Say what you will, but that head-shaking looked more like a threat to the visitors than an expression of grief.

He looked suspiciously at the deceased lying next to his sister and, after moving his head and the fingers of his left hand questioningly in an oriental manner, turned to the student:
— Hey, what is this business? Why have they put   t h a t   o n e   here? What is a man doing in the boarding house?
— Shh! I beg you, Mr. Ganyo, speak more quietly.
— Why take it easy, huh? I'm spending money here! Where's the director?
— This is not the boarding house, this is a private house — answers the stunned student.
— Like a private house?
— Shh... For God's sake, speak more quietly! — implored the unfortunate student, deafened by the blood rushing to his head, ready to cry.

Regardless of the swaggering behavior and manners of Bay Ganyo, which had already come to resemble sacrilege, a mockery of the sacred feelings of all those around him, his very outward appearance as well did not at all inspire sympathy in the Americans and the English, and especially in their fairer half.

Bay Ganyo was dressed in grayish-brown homespun clothes, with uncleaned, dusty boots, his neck tied with a large mourning scarf, under which a rather grimy shirt, unbuttoned in the middle, could be seen. In his hand a walking stick and under his arm a package, wrapped in yellow paper. His mustache was again twisted, and his beard again unshaven — overgrown.
— Is this gentleman Mademoiselle Marie's brother? — one of the household asked me.

I answered him in the affirmative, adding as an excuse for Bai Ganyo’s behavior and appearance a hastily concocted lie: I told him that the telegram with the sorrowful news had found Bai Ganyo at his estate while he was overseeing his field work, and that without stopping at his villa (Bai Ganyo and a villa!), he had gone to the railway, obtained money from acquaintances at the station, and come to Dresden without stopping anywhere. And his current behavior, though it may seem strange, should be forgiven him, considering the overwhelming impression made upon him by the irreplaceable loss of his sister and... the enormous losses he is suffering from the untimely abandonment of his field work.
— Oh, the poor man! — my interlocutor said sympathetically and went to share his feelings about Bai Ganyo with the other members of the household and friends.

My heart felt a bit lighter, gentlemen! But it felt lighter for only a very short time. The American, the host, had already managed to convey the information gathered from me to a large part of those present; their noble indignation, provoked by Bay Ganyo’s manners, had subsided, and everyone looked upon Bay Ganyo not only favorably but also sympathetically: an unexpectedly arrived terrible telegram, an unprepared departure for a long journey, enormous losses—these are such surprises that can leave anyone stunned. And with these surprises, they indulgently excused Bay Ganyo.

But, gentlemen, tell me, I pray you, with what could we, the Bulgarian students, justify the following action of Bay Ganyo? The student, who was hovering around him to restrain the outburst of his feelings, was quietly telling him how the catastrophe in the cliffs of Saxon Switzerland had occurred. During this narration, Bay Ganyo expressed with various movements of his head and hands the feelings that agitated him: now clicking his tongue and letting out a: “Tsk, if only it hadn't happened!”; now looking at his sister and shaking his head: “the poor soul!”; now looking at the deceased youth, shaking his head threateningly, his eyes flashing like lightning as if to say: “At the very least, this lout has gotten into... some fine mess.” The foreigners interpreted these facial expressions in their own way and hardly guessed their true meaning, for otherwise they would not have looked so sympathetically at Bay Ganyo, whom they considered to be deranged by grief.

At one point, Bay Ganyo, under the impression of the story, clicked his tongue so loudly that everyone turned their eyes toward him. At that very moment, he applied the thumb of his right hand to his right nostril, twisted his eyes and mouth slightly to the right, bowed his head a bit, and blew through his left nostril... Then he applied his left finger to the other nostril and let it rip once more... We were utterly mortified...

You might say that this, too, could be excused by the haste of his departure: the poor fellow, you will say, in his rush and confusion, forgot even to take a handkerchief. But it is not so! It is not, because immediately after this operation, Bai Ganyo unwrapped the package with the yellow paper and took out—what do you think?—a whole dozen handkerchiefs and began to distribute them to those present, primarily to the Bulgarians, for "God rest her soul," repeating as he handed them over: "Here, you take one too, and say God rest her soul"; or he would wave his hand for someone to approach and shout to him: "Hey, boy, come here, here’s one for you too, come on, and say God rest her soul, M a r i y k a"...

— I won't tell you any more, gentlemen — Kolyo cried out in despair, — try for yourselves to imagine the faces of the English and Americans who surrounded Bay Ganyo. I will only tell you that after the funeral service for the deceased as an Orthodox in the Russian church was over and after we buried her, Bay Ganyo was invited to stay at the Americans' home until his departure from Dresden. He spent only one night there. What kind of behavior he maintained in that house — I do not know. Only upon leaving did he say to the Bulgarian student who was seeing him off at the station: — Forget it, brother, I almost made a real mess of things. I don't know the ways of these Americans: food galore, for free, so I ate and ate, I was about to burst from eating; and then during the night... Forget it!... But leave that aside, here's another blunder: a woman comes in the morning, you see, knocks on the door. I say — "Come in!" She enters, brings me coffee with milk and various sweets. She puts the tray on the table, you see, and starts sniffing the air with her nose. — The devil take it! Did she smell the rose oil, or something else! — I, you know, I'm no fool, I get up immediately, take the vial and shove it under her nose. She smiled a bit. I look at her — not bad! Dressed simply like that, I thought to myself, a servant. I gave her a wink — she's laughing! And I — hop! — around the waist. But then she spun around, damn her, and she slapped me across the face... forget it, I was mortified!... It turns out she was the boy's aunt... Anyway, thank goodness, it ended with just one slap. Good people!...
